name: Ming China
title: Social Hierarchy of Ming China: From Emperor to the Enslaved

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You stand above every law and rank and choose your ministers, and you may stay unseen in the Forbidden City for years, while officials bribe your eunuchs to have their messages carried to you.
tiers.kid: The emperor ruled all of China from the Forbidden City in Beijing, with ministers and palace servants to help him.
tiers.rise: The throne passed within the founder’s house, and the reigning emperor named his heir: the Hongwu Emperor chose his grandson. It could also be won by war, as the Yongle Emperor took it from his nephew in 1402, and lost by capture: when the Oirats seized the Zhengtong Emperor in 1449 his brother took the throne, and he won it back only by a coup in 1457.
tiers.why: The emperor stood on a social and legal tier above everyone else, embodying a heavenly mandate to judicial and executive authority.

tiers.name: Imperial princes
tiers.you: You are a prince of the imperial house, with the title of king, a stipend and a great estate far from the northern border, but no say at all in the government.
tiers.kid: The emperor’s relatives were made princes with big estates and pay, but they were not allowed to govern.
tiers.rise: Princely rank came by descent from the founder, and the emperor could take a prince’s power away, as Yongle did his brothers’. Only near the end of the dynasty were some princes allowed to sit the examinations and serve as officials.
tiers.why: Descendants of the first Ming emperor were made princes and given military commands, usually nominal, annual stipends and large estates.

tiers.name: Officials
tiers.you: You passed the palace examination and are a jinshi; you govern a county far from your home district, your superiors grade you every three years, and a censor may impeach you at any time.
tiers.kid: Officials who had passed very hard exams on old books ran the government, from ministers to county magistrates.
tiers.rise: Office came through the examinations: provincial graduates began in low posts, while those who passed the palace examination became jinshi and were assured high positions. There were only two to four thousand jinshi at any time, “on the order of one out of 10,000 adult males”, in Ebrey’s words.
tiers.why: After 1384, when the founder stopped staffing his bureaus by recommendation only, the officials were recruited through the examinations.

tiers.name: Palace eunuchs
tiers.you: You were castrated as a boy to win a place in the palace; now you manage an imperial workshop, and if you win the emperor’s trust, officials will need your favour to reach him.
tiers.kid: Palace servants called eunuchs ran the emperor’s household, and some became more powerful than his ministers.
tiers.rise: Many men castrated themselves for a place in the palace or in an official’s household, for them the only way into a life of privilege; others were prisoners of war, tribute from neighbouring lands, or boys punished for their fathers’ crimes. A few rose to rule the court, as Wang Zhen, Liu Jin and Wei Zhongxian did.
tiers.why: Eunuchs gained unprecedented power under the Ming.

tiers.name: The degree-holding gentry
tiers.you: You have passed the first examination and are a shengyuan: you teach in a private school, advise the magistrate on local projects and practise the eight-legged essay for the provincial examination.
tiers.kid: Men who passed the first exams became gentry, the leaders of their towns and villages.
tiers.rise: In theory anyone could sit the examinations, which were graded without regard to background, but the years of costly tutoring confined success to families of means: 90 per cent of the population was ineligible for lack of education, while the upper 10 per cent had equal chances. Provincial quotas curbed the hold of the landholding gentry of the most prosperous regions.
tiers.why: Below the officials stood the gentry, landholding families whose men had earned examination degrees: by the 16th century some 100,000 shengyuan, “government students”, the lowest tier of graduates, with the provincial…

tiers.name: Soldiers and military households
tiers.you: You were born into a soldier household of a frontier garrison: you farm your military plot, serve when you are called, and your sons will serve after you.
tiers.kid: Soldier families farmed land near their forts and served in the army, generation after generation.
tiers.rise: Soldier households were bound to service by birth, and many deserted; yet for a man without formal education the army was the quickest road to power, and officers could sit the civil examinations, or from 1478 the military’s own.
tiers.why: The Hongwu Emperor built a standing army of more than a million men on the weisuo system: hereditary soldier households in garrisons (wei) and battalions (suo), settled on their own farm lots so that the army would…

tiers.name: Buddhist and Daoist clergy
tiers.you: You are a Daoist priest in one of the state’s ritual offices, registered by the Ministry of Rites, and the emperor himself favours your teaching over the Buddhists’.
tiers.kid: Buddhist monks and Daoist priests looked after temples, and the government kept lists of them.
tiers.rise: The monastic life’s exemption from tax had long drawn poor farmers to it; the state answered with registers and, at times, persecution.
tiers.why: Monks and priests stood outside the four occupations; a Song official had counted Buddhist monks as a sixth category beside them.

tiers.name: Farmers
tiers.you: You own a small farm north of the Huai River, grow wheat and millet, pay the land tax in silver and live not far above subsistence.
tiers.kid: Most people were farmers who grew rice, wheat, tea or silk and paid taxes to the emperor.
tiers.rise: A prospering family could pay for a son’s schooling, though the cost kept most out of the examinations. In hard times farmers went to the cities for work, and many left their registered homes to wander, until the Jiajing Emperor had officials register migrants wherever they had moved.
tiers.why: Farmers ranked second in theory, after the scholars, as the primary creators of wealth, and the land tax on their plots produced much of the state’s revenue.

tiers.name: Artisans
tiers.you: You work for wages in a small weaving workshop under a master craftsman, and you belong to your craft’s guild.
tiers.kid: Craftspeople made silk, paper and blue-and-white porcelain, some of it sold as far away as Europe.
tiers.rise: A skilled artisan could gain enough capital to hire apprentices and labourers and run a small enterprise; occupations could be chosen or inherited, for the four occupations were not hereditary.
tiers.why: Artisans came third in the four occupations, respected more than merchants in theory because they made useful things, though, often having no land of their own, they paid little to the state.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You trade salt under a licence won by shipping grain to the northern garrisons, and you have bought books on proper conduct so that your family will be received among the gentry.
tiers.kid: Merchants were ranked last in old ideas, but many grew rich trading salt, silk and tea.
tiers.rise: Wealth carried a merchant’s family toward the gentry: merchants funded schools and imitated the scholars, the sumptuary laws were no longer enforced from the mid-Ming, and in some regions scholars switched to careers in trade.
tiers.why: Merchants stood last in theory, distrusted for piling up wealth, and the early Ming sumptuary laws barred them and their families from wearing silk; it was frowned upon for merchants to sit the examinations.

tiers.name: The mean people
tiers.you: You sing in a teahouse of the city: wealthy men admire your art, but the law counts you among the mean people, below every farmer and craftsman.
tiers.kid: Entertainers such as musicians and dancers were looked down on by law, even when audiences loved them.
tiers.rise: A few dancers rose by becoming concubines, but the law kept the mean people apart: to give entertainers official recognition would have given them more prestige.
tiers.why: Beneath the four occupations were the “mean people” (jianmin), set against the “good people” (liangmin): those whose work was thought worthless or “filthy”, entertainers and prostitutes above all.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: Your poor parents gave you up to a rich household as an “adopted” child, and now you belong to that household as a servant.
tiers.kid: Some people were enslaved, often as a punishment for crimes, even though the first Ming emperor tried to end slavery.
tiers.rise: People fell into slavery by a criminal sentence, by the sale of poor children disguised as adoption, or as captives of war and rebellion.
tiers.why: Slavery was comparatively uncommon in Chinese history and was practised largely as a judicial punishment for crimes.
